source_refs.note: Topic 21.3.2 (PDF 81-82); the E2 and E1 schemes are redrawn. The book's E1 carbocation is drawn with a CH2 group; it is (CH3)3C+.

blocks.text: Beta-elimination is a reaction in which a hydrogen atom on the beta carbon (the carbon next to the one carrying the halogen) and the halogen atom are removed. It happens when a base attacks the beta hydrogen; the halogen leaves at the same time or afterwards, and an alkene forms instead of a substitution product. Elimination takes place alongside substitution and often competes with it. Like substitution, it can follow two mechanisms, E2 or E1.

items: E2 (bimolecular): the base attacks the beta hydrogen and the leaving group departs at the same time as the C=C double bond forms, in one step. The rate depends on both the halogenoalkane and the base: rate = k[halogenoalkane][base], second order.

blocks.alt: Base- with a curly arrow to a beta H of bromoethane, a curly arrow from that C-H bond to the C-C bond, and a curly arrow from the C-Br bond to Br, giving ethene + H-Base + Br-.
blocks.caption: E2 mechanism: bromoethane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 81).

items: E1 (unimolecular): like SN1, the first step is the slow ionisation of the substrate to a carbocation; in the second step the base removes a beta hydrogen to give the alkene. The rate depends only on the halogenoalkane: rate = k[halogenoalkane].

blocks.alt: Step 1: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (delta+ C, delta- Br) with equilibrium arrows marked slow gives the 3 degree carbocation + Br-. Step 2: Base- with a curly arrow to a beta H, and a curly arrow from that C-H bond to the bond to the positive carbon, fast, gives 2-methylpropene + H-Base.
blocks.caption: E1 mechanism: 2-bromo-2-methylpropane (original drawing after the textbook's unnumbered figure on PDF page 81).

blocks.text: Primary halogenoalkanes generally follow E2 and tertiary halogenoalkanes E1, while secondary halogenoalkanes can show either, depending on the solvent.
